claim: In mice, neonatally-developing, self-reactive B-1 cells generate steady levels of natural antibodies throughout life.
source: In mice, neonatally-developing, self-reactive B-1 cells generate steady levels of natural antibodies throughout life.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that is supported by citations and established knowledge in the field.

claim: B-1 cells can rapidly respond to infections with increased local antibody production.
source: B-1 cells can, however, also rapidly respond to infections with increased local antibody production.
evidence: This statement is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript and prior citations.

claim: The mechanisms regulating natural antibody production and infection responses by B-1 cells are poorly understood.
source: The mechanisms regulating these two seemingly very distinct functions are poorly understood, but have been linked to expression of CD5, an inhibitor of BCR-signaling.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field, supported by the literature context.

claim: CD5 is an inhibitor of BCR-signaling.
source: The mechanisms regulating these two seemingly very distinct functions are poorly understood, but have been linked to expression of CD5, an inhibitor of BCR-signaling.
evidence: This is supported by citations in the introduction and established knowledge.

claim: TLR-mediated activation of CD5+ B-1 cells induces rapid reorganization of the IgM-BCR complex.
source: Here we demonstrate that TLR-mediated activation of CD5+ B-1 cells induced the rapid reorganization of the IgM-BCR complex, leading to the eventual loss of CD5 expression, and a concomitant increase in BCR-downstream signaling, both in vitro and in vivo after infections of mice with influenza virus and Salmonella typhimurium.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data including PLA assays and flow cytometry.

claim: TLR-mediated activation of CD5+ B-1 cells leads to the eventual loss of CD5 expression.
source: Here we demonstrate that TLR-mediated activation of CD5+ B-1 cells induced the rapid reorganization of the IgM-BCR complex, leading to the eventual loss of CD5 expression, and a concomitant increase in BCR-downstream signaling, both in vitro and in vivo after infections of mice with influenza virus and Salmonella typhimurium.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data showing CD5 downregulation after LPS and other TLR agonist stimulation.

claim: TLR-mediated activation of CD5+ B-1 cells results in a concomitant increase in BCR-downstream signaling.
source: Here we demonstrate that TLR-mediated activation of CD5+ B-1 cells induced the rapid reorganization of the IgM-BCR complex, leading to the eventual loss of CD5 expression, and a concomitant increase in BCR-downstream signaling, both in vitro and in vivo after infections of mice with influenza virus and Salmonella typhimurium.
evidence: This is supported by PLA data showing increased CD79:Syk interactions and phospho-Akt measurements.

claim: Both initial CD5 expression and TLR-mediated stimulation are required for the differentiation of B-1 cells to IgM-producing plasmablasts after infections.
source: Both, initial CD5 expression and TLR-mediated stimulation, were required for the differentiation of B-1 cells to IgM-producing plasmablasts after infections.
evidence: This is supported by experiments using neonatal chimeras with CD5+ vs CD5- B-1 cells and TLR-deficient mice.

claim: TLR-mediated signals support participation of B-1 cells in immune defense via BCR-complex reorganization.
source: Thus, TLR-mediated signals support participation of B-1 cells in immune defense via BCR-complex reorganization.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Self-antigen binding by the TCR and BCR during lymphocyte development results in negative selection.
source: During lymphocyte development (self)-antigen binding by the TCR and BCR results in negative selection, leading to the removal of strongly self-reactive lymphocytes from the T and B cell repertoire.
evidence: This is established immunological knowledge supported by the citation (Melchers, 2015).

claim: Self-reactive B cells undergo deletion, receptor-editing, or become anergic depending on the strength of antigen-BCR interactions.
source: Depending on the strengths of these antigen-BCR interactions, self-reactive B cells undergo deletion, receptor-editing, or they become anergic, that is unresponsive to antigen-receptor engagement (Melchers, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the citation and represents established knowledge in B cell biology.

claim: Self-reactive, anergic bone marrow-derived B cells up-regulate expression of the signaling inhibitor CD5.
source: Self-reactive, anergic bone marrow-derived B cells up-regulate expression of the signaling inhibitor CD5 (Hippen et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Hippen et al., 2000.

claim: On developing T cells, the levels of CD5 expression correlate with TCR signaling intensity encountered during thymic development.
source: On developing T cells, the levels of CD5 expression correlate with TCR signaling intensity encountered during thymic development, with those most strongly binding to self-antigens expressing the highest levels of CD5 (Punt et al., 1994; Azzam et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by the citations to Punt et al., 1994 and Azzam et al., 1998.

claim: T cells most strongly binding to self-antigens express the highest levels of CD5.
source: On developing T cells, the levels of CD5 expression correlate with TCR signaling intensity encountered during thymic development, with those most strongly binding to self-antigens expressing the highest levels of CD5 (Punt et al., 1994; Azzam et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by the citations to Punt et al., 1994 and Azzam et al., 1998.

claim: Several ligands have been proposed for CD5.
source: While several ligands have been proposed for CD5 (Punt et al., 1994; Berland and Wortis, 2002; Biancone et al., 1996; Bikah et al., 1998; Brown and Lacey, 2010; Calvo et al., 1999; Pospisil et al., 1996; Van de Velde et al., 1991), none seem to have significant CD5-dependent biological effects.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: None of the proposed CD5 ligands seem to have significant CD5-dependent biological effects.
source: While several ligands have been proposed for CD5 (Punt et al., 1994; Berland and Wortis, 2002; Biancone et al., 1996; Bikah et al., 1998; Brown and Lacey, 2010; Calvo et al., 1999; Pospisil et al., 1996; Van de Velde et al., 1991), none seem to have significant CD5-dependent biological effects.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited literature.

claim: Most B-1 cells express CD5.
source: In addition to anergic B cells, most B-1 cells also express CD5.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field and supported by the data in the manuscript.

claim: B-1 cells are primarily fetal and neonatal-derived.
source: In contrast to lymphocytes developing postnatal, these primarily fetal and neonatal-derived B cells (Yuan et al., 2012; Zhou et al., 2015; Hardy and Hayakawa, 2001) seem to undergo a positive selection step during development, requiring self-antigen recognition and strong BCR signaling.
evidence: This is supported by the citations to Yuan et al., 2012; Zhou et al., 2015; Hardy and Hayakawa, 2001.

claim: B-1 cells undergo a positive selection step during development, requiring self-antigen recognition and strong BCR signaling.
source: In contrast to lymphocytes developing postnatal, these primarily fetal and neonatal-derived B cells (Yuan et al., 2012; Zhou et al., 2015; Hardy and Hayakawa, 2001) seem to undergo a positive selection step during development, requiring self-antigen recognition and strong BCR signaling.
evidence: This is supported by the citations and established knowledge in B-1 cell biology.

claim: The lack of self-antigen expression diminished B-1 cell development.
source: The lack of self-antigen expression, or the deletion of co-stimulatory molecules that enhance BCR signaling, diminished B-1 cell development, while deletion of negative co-stimulatory signals, or enhanced surface expression of the BCR, resulted in enhanced B-1a cell development (Berland and Wortis, 2002; Hardy and Hayakawa, 2001; Casola et al., 2004; Hayakawa and Hardy, 2000; Nguyen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Deletion of co-stimulatory molecules that enhance BCR signaling diminished B-1 cell development.
source: The lack of self-antigen expression, or the deletion of co-stimulatory molecules that enhance BCR signaling, diminished B-1 cell development, while deletion of negative co-stimulatory signals, or enhanced surface expression of the BCR, resulted in enhanced B-1a cell development (Berland and Wortis, 2002; Hardy and Hayakawa, 2001; Casola et al., 2004; Hayakawa and Hardy, 2000; Nguyen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Deletion of negative co-stimulatory signals resulted in enhanced B-1a cell development.
source: The lack of self-antigen expression, or the deletion of co-stimulatory molecules that enhance BCR signaling, diminished B-1 cell development, while deletion of negative co-stimulatory signals, or enhanced surface expression of the BCR, resulted in enhanced B-1a cell development (Berland and Wortis, 2002; Hardy and Hayakawa, 2001; Casola et al., 2004; Hayakawa and Hardy, 2000; Nguyen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Enhanced surface expression of the BCR resulted in enhanced B-1a cell development.
source: The lack of self-antigen expression, or the deletion of co-stimulatory molecules that enhance BCR signaling, diminished B-1 cell development, while deletion of negative co-stimulatory signals, or enhanced surface expression of the BCR, resulted in enhanced B-1a cell development (Berland and Wortis, 2002; Hardy and Hayakawa, 2001; Casola et al., 2004; Hayakawa and Hardy, 2000; Nguyen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: CD5+ B-1 cells have a self-reactive BCR repertoire.
source: Specificity of CD5+ B-1 cells for self-antigens and self-antigen binding during development is consistent with their known self-reactive BCR repertoire (Hayakawa et al., 1999; Lalor and Morahan, 1990; Mercolino et al., 1988; Yang et al., 2015) and thus a role for CD5 in silencing B-1 cell responses to BCR-engagement in order to avert autoimmune responses.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: CD5 silences B-1 cell responses to BCR-engagement in order to avert autoimmune responses.
source: Specificity of CD5+ B-1 cells for self-antigens and self-antigen binding during development is consistent with their known self-reactive BCR repertoire (Hayakawa et al., 1999; Lalor and Morahan, 1990; Mercolino et al., 1988; Yang et al., 2015) and thus a role for CD5 in silencing B-1 cell responses to BCR-engagement in order to avert autoimmune responses.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited literature and the known function of CD5.

claim: B-1 cells are divided into two subsets, B-1a and B-1b, based on their expression of CD5.
source: Yet, not all B-1 cells express CD5, instead depending on their expression or not of CD5, they are typically divided into two subsets, B-1a and B-1b, respectively.
evidence: This is established nomenclature in the field.

claim: B-1a cells do not proliferate in response to BCR stimulation.
source: In contrast to B-1b cells, and consistent with their expression of CD5, B-1a cells do not proliferate in response to BCR stimulation (Morris and Rothstein, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Morris and Rothstein, 1993 and the data in Figure 5B.

claim: In CD5-/- mice, mature B-1 cells demonstrated a proliferative response similar to that of conventional B (B-2) cells.
source: However, in CD5-/- mice and in mice in which the association of membrane IgM with CD5 was inhibited, mature B-1 cells demonstrated a proliferative response similar to that of conventional B (B-2) cells (Tarakhovsky et al., 1994; Bikah et al., 1996), further confirming that CD5 expression reduces B-1 cell responsiveness to BCR-signaling.
evidence: This is supported by the citations to Tarakhovsky et al., 1994 and Bikah et al., 1996.

claim: In mice in which the association of membrane IgM with CD5 was inhibited, mature B-1 cells demonstrated a proliferative response similar to that of conventional B (B-2) cells.
source: However, in CD5-/- mice and in mice in which the association of membrane IgM with CD5 was inhibited, mature B-1 cells demonstrated a proliferative response similar to that of conventional B (B-2) cells (Tarakhovsky et al., 1994; Bikah et al., 1996), further confirming that CD5 expression reduces B-1 cell responsiveness to BCR-signaling.
evidence: This is supported by the citations to Tarakhovsky et al., 1994 and Bikah et al., 1996.

claim: CD5 expression reduces B-1 cell responsiveness to BCR-signaling.
source: However, in CD5-/- mice and in mice in which the association of membrane IgM with CD5 was inhibited, mature B-1 cells demonstrated a proliferative response similar to that of conventional B (B-2) cells (Tarakhovsky et al., 1994; Bikah et al., 1996), further confirming that CD5 expression reduces B-1 cell responsiveness to BCR-signaling.
evidence: This is supported by the citations and the experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: B-1 cells strongly respond to innate, TLR-mediated signals, such as LPS.
source: A BCR-signaling independent response of B-1 cells might be inferred from the fact that B-1 cells strongly respond to innate, TLR-mediated signals, such as LPS, and that they are a major source for 'natural' self-reactive IgM.
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figures 2 and 3 showing B-1 cell responses to LPS and other TLR agonists.

claim: B-1 cells are a major source for 'natural' self-reactive IgM.
source: A BCR-signaling independent response of B-1 cells might be inferred from the fact that B-1 cells strongly respond to innate, TLR-mediated signals, such as LPS, and that they are a major source for 'natural' self-reactive IgM.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Steady-state secretion of natural IgM does not appear to require external antigenic stimulation.
source: Moreover, steady-state secretion of natural IgM does not appear to require external antigenic stimulation, as total serum levels of natural IgM and frequencies of IgM-secreting B-1 cells are similar in mice held under both, SPF and germfree housing conditions (Baumgarth et al., 2015; Ochsenbein et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by the citations to Baumgarth et al., 2015 and Ochsenbein et al., 1999.

claim: Total serum levels of natural IgM are similar in mice held under SPF and germfree housing conditions.
source: Moreover, steady-state secretion of natural IgM does not appear to require external antigenic stimulation, as total serum levels of natural IgM and frequencies of IgM-secreting B-1 cells are similar in mice held under both, SPF and germfree housing conditions (Baumgarth et al., 2015; Ochsenbein et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by the citations to Baumgarth et al., 2015 and Ochsenbein et al., 1999.

claim: Frequencies of IgM-secreting B-1 cells are similar in mice held under SPF and germfree housing conditions.

evidence: This is supported by the citations to Baumgarth et al., 2015 and Ochsenbein et al., 1999.

claim: Natural IgM production is not stochastic, but instead likely driven by expression of self-antigens.
source: However, natural IgM production is not stochastic, but instead likely driven by expression of self-antigens.
evidence: This is supported by the subsequent citations to Hayakawa et al. and Yang et al.

claim: Thy-1-deficient mice lack anti-Thy-1 self-reactive IgM antibodies in their serum.
source: This was demonstrated by Hayakawa et al, who showed a lack of anti-Thy-1 self-reactive IgM antibodies in the serum of Thy-1-deficient but not Thy-1 expressing mice (Hayakawa et al., 1999; Hayakawa et al., 2003), as well as repertoire studies by Yang et al, which showed selective and extensive clonal expansion of certain CD5+ B-1 cell clones during the first 6 months of life, including in germfree mice (Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the citations to Hayakawa et al., 1999 and Hayakawa et al., 2003.

claim: Thy-1 expressing mice have anti-Thy-1 self-reactive IgM antibodies in their serum.
source: This was demonstrated by Hayakawa et al, who showed a lack of anti-Thy-1 self-reactive IgM antibodies in the serum of Thy-1-deficient but not Thy-1 expressing mice (Hayakawa et al., 1999; Hayakawa et al., 2003), as well as repertoire studies by Yang et al, which showed selective and extensive clonal expansion of certain CD5+ B-1 cell clones during the first 6 months of life, including in germfree mice (Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is implied by the contrast with Thy-1-deficient mice and supported by the citations.

claim: Certain CD5+ B-1 cell clones undergo selective and extensive clonal expansion during the first 6 months of life.
source: This was demonstrated by Hayakawa et al, who showed a lack of anti-Thy-1 self-reactive IgM antibodies in the serum of Thy-1-deficient but not Thy-1 expressing mice (Hayakawa et al., 1999; Hayakawa et al., 2003), as well as repertoire studies by Yang et al, which showed selective and extensive clonal expansion of certain CD5+ B-1 cell clones during the first 6 months of life, including in germfree mice (Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Yang et al., 2015.

claim: Certain CD5+ B-1 cell clones undergo selective and extensive clonal expansion in germfree mice.
source: This was demonstrated by Hayakawa et al, who showed a lack of anti-Thy-1 self-reactive IgM antibodies in the serum of Thy-1-deficient but not Thy-1 expressing mice (Hayakawa et al., 1999; Hayakawa et al., 2003), as well as repertoire studies by Yang et al, which showed selective and extensive clonal expansion of certain CD5+ B-1 cell clones during the first 6 months of life, including in germfree mice (Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Yang et al., 2015.

claim: B-1 cells can be actively involved in immune responses to various pathogens.
source: Furthermore, B-1 cells can be also actively involved in immune responses to various pathogens (Haas et al., 2005; Alugupalli et al., 2003; Alugupalli et al., 2004; Gil-Cruz et al., 2009; Choi and Baumgarth, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: CD5- B-1b cells, but not B-1a cells, respond to pathogen encounters in an antigen-dependent manner.
source: Given that CD5 is a BCR inhibitor, it was suggested that CD5- B-1b cells, but not B-1a cells, respond to pathogen encounters in an antigen-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a previously suggested model in the field, which the current manuscript challenges.

claim: CD19-deficient mice lack B-1a development.
source: Haas and colleagues, conducting studies in CD19-deficient mice that lack B-1a development, concluded that B-1a cells are responsible for natural IgM secretion, while only the B-1b cells responded to Streptococcus pneumonia infection (Haas et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Haas et al., 2005.

claim: B-1a cells are responsible for natural IgM secretion.
source: Haas and colleagues, conducting studies in CD19-deficient mice that lack B-1a development, concluded that B-1a cells are responsible for natural IgM secretion, while only the B-1b cells responded to Streptococcus pneumonia infection (Haas et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a conclusion from Haas et al., 2005, which the current manuscript reinterprets.

claim: Only B-1b cells responded to Streptococcus pneumonia infection.
source: Haas and colleagues, conducting studies in CD19-deficient mice that lack B-1a development, concluded that B-1a cells are responsible for natural IgM secretion, while only the B-1b cells responded to Streptococcus pneumonia infection (Haas et al., 2005).

claim: CD5- B-1b cells expand and secrete protective IgM after infection with Borrelia hermsii.
source: Similarly, CD5- B-1b cells were shown to expand and secrete protective IgM after infection with Borrelia hermsii and Salmonella typhimurium (Alugupalli et al., 2003; Alugupalli et al., 2004; Gil-Cruz et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by the citations, though the current manuscript reinterprets these findings.

claim: CD5- B-1b cells expand and secrete protective IgM after infection with Salmonella typhimurium.
source: Similarly, CD5- B-1b cells were shown to expand and secrete protective IgM after infection with Borrelia hermsii and Salmonella typhimurium (Alugupalli et al., 2003; Alugupalli et al., 2004; Gil-Cruz et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by the citations, though the current manuscript reinterprets these findings.

claim: Only CD5+ B-1 cells respond in vivo to influenza infection with migration from the pleural cavity to the draining mediastinal lymph nodes.
source: Chimeric mice reconstituted with either allotypically-marked CD5+ or CD5- B-1 cells showed that only CD5+ B-1 cells were responding in vivo to influenza infection with migration from the pleural cavity to the draining mediastinal lymph nodes (MedLN) in a Type I IFN-dependent process, where they differentiated into IgM-secreting cells (Choi and Baumgarth, 2008; Waffarn et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the citations to Choi and Baumgarth, 2008 and Waffarn et al., 2015.

claim: CD5+ B-1 cells migrate from the pleural cavity to the MedLN in a Type I IFN-dependent process after influenza infection.
source: Chimeric mice reconstituted with either allotypically-marked CD5+ or CD5- B-1 cells showed that only CD5+ B-1 cells were responding in vivo to influenza infection with migration from the pleural cavity to the draining mediastinal lymph nodes (MedLN) in a Type I IFN-dependent process, where they differentiated into IgM-secreting cells (Choi and Baumgarth, 2008; Waffarn et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the citations to Choi and Baumgarth, 2008 and Waffarn et al., 2015.

claim: CD5+ B-1 cells differentiate into IgM-secreting cells in the MedLN after influenza infection.
source: Chimeric mice reconstituted with either allotypically-marked CD5+ or CD5- B-1 cells showed that only CD5+ B-1 cells were responding in vivo to influenza infection with migration from the pleural cavity to the draining mediastinal lymph nodes (MedLN) in a Type I IFN-dependent process, where they differentiated into IgM-secreting cells (Choi and Baumgarth, 2008; Waffarn et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the citations and the data in Figure 1.

claim: CD5+ B-1 cells respond to influenza virus infection.
source: This study addresses some of these questions and reconciles previous divergent findings on B-1 cell responses to infections by demonstrating that only CD5+ B-1 cells respond to influenza virus as well as Salmonella infections, but that once activated, these B-1 cells lose expression of CD5 and thus become 'B-1b' like.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by the data in Figures 1 and 4.

claim: CD5+ B-1 cells respond to Salmonella infections.
source: This study addresses some of these questions and reconciles previous divergent findings on B-1 cell responses to infections by demonstrating that only CD5+ B-1 cells respond to influenza virus as well as Salmonella infections, but that once activated, these B-1 cells lose expression of CD5 and thus become 'B-1b' like.

evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by the data in Figures 1-4.

claim: TLR triggering results in the reorganization of the IgM-BCR complex.
source: Mechanistically, the downregulation of CD5 requires expression of TLR, triggering of which resulted in the reorganization of the IgM-BCR complex.
evidence: This is supported by the PLA data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: BCR reorganization led to the rapid dissociation of CD5 from the IgM-BCR complex.
source: BCR reorganization led to the rapid dissociation, and then eventual loss of CD5 from the complex, and triggered enhanced IgM-CD19 and CD79:Syk interactions, resulting in enhanced down-stream BCR-signaling.
evidence: This is supported by the PLA data in Figure 6A.

claim: BCR reorganization triggered enhanced IgM-CD19 interactions.
source: BCR reorganization led to the rapid dissociation, and then eventual loss of CD5 from the complex, and triggered enhanced IgM-CD19 and CD79:Syk interactions, resulting in enhanced down-stream BCR-signaling.
evidence: This is supported by the PLA data in Figure 6A.

claim: BCR reorganization triggered enhanced CD79:Syk interactions.
source: BCR reorganization led to the rapid dissociation, and then eventual loss of CD5 from the complex, and triggered enhanced IgM-CD19 and CD79:Syk interactions, resulting in enhanced down-stream BCR-signaling.
evidence: This is supported by the PLA data in Figure 6A.

claim: BCR reorganization resulted in enhanced down-stream BCR-signaling.
source: BCR reorganization led to the rapid dissociation, and then eventual loss of CD5 from the complex, and triggered enhanced IgM-CD19 and CD79:Syk interactions, resulting in enhanced down-stream BCR-signaling.
evidence: This is supported by the phospho-Akt data in Figure 6B and Nur77 expression in Figure 6C.

claim: B-1 cells migrated to MedLN and rapidly differentiated to IgM-secreting B-1PC on day seven after infection with influenza A Puerto Rico 8/34.
source: Examination of the MedLN of neonatal chimeras showed that B-1 cells migrated to MedLN and then rapidly differentiated to IgM-secreting B-1PC on day seven after infection with influenza A Puerto Rico 8/34 (A/PR8) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the FACS data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Blimp-1-YFP+ B-1PC are present in the MedLN after influenza infection.
source: Neonatal chimeric mice generated with B-1 donor cells from Blimp-1 YFP reporter mice (Fooksman et al., 2010; Rutishauser et al., 2009) confirmed the presence of Blimp-1-YFP+ B-1PC in the MedLN (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: MedLN B-1PC mostly lacked expression of CD5, particularly among the Blimp-1hi cells.
source: The MedLN B-1PC mostly lacked expression of CD5, particularly among the Blimp-1hi cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the FACS data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: CD5+ Blimp-1-YFP+ cells expressed less Blimp-1-YFP than the CD5- Blimp-1-YFP+ B-1 cells.
source: Also, the CD5+ Blimp-1-YFP+ cells expressed less Blimp-1-YFP than the CD5- Blimp-1-YFP+ B-1 cells (Figure 1C, left).
evidence: This is supported by the FACS data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: CD5- cells secreted more IgM compared to the CD5+ cells after influenza infection.
source: Consistent with the presence of CD5- B-1PC, the CD5- cells secreted more IgM compared to the CD5+ cells, measuring total IgM concentrations and calculating IgM production per cell (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by the ELISA data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Sorted CD5+ cells did not secrete measurable amounts of IgM unless harvested after day 5 of infection.
source: Sorted CD5+ cells did not secrete measurable amounts of IgM unless harvested after day 5 of infection.
evidence: This is supported by the ELISA data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: About 70% of CD19hiIgMb+IgDloCD43+B-1 cells in the MedLN expressed CD5 after influenza infection.
source: The studies confirmed our previous findings that among CD19hiIgMb+IgDloCD43+B-1 cells in the MedLN, about 70% expressed CD5 after influenza infection (Figure 1F–G).
evidence: This is supported by the FACS data shown in Figure 1F-G.

claim: The frequency of CD5 negative MedLN B-1 cells increased after influenza infection.
source: In contrast to the analysis described above, this expanded analysis of all B-1 donor Igh-b cells revealed that the frequency of CD5 negative MedLN B-1 cells increased after influenza infection (Figure 1H–I), consistent with the development of CD5- B-1PC in this compartment (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by the FACS data shown in Figure 1H-I.

claim: A higher frequency and total number of CD5- B-1 cells secreted IgM in the MedLN compared to CD5+ B-1 cells on days 3, 5, and seven after infection.
source: Furthermore, FACS-sorting and culture of CD5+ and CD5- B-1 cells showed that a higher frequency and total number of CD5- B-1 cells secreted IgM in the MedLN compared to CD5+ B-1 cells on days 3, 5, and seven after infection (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is supported by the ELISPOT data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Approximately 40% of highly purified FACS-sorted CD5+ B-1 cells from the peritoneal cavity lacked CD5 expression when cultured for 3 days in the presence of LPS.
source: Indeed, approximately 40% of highly purified FACS-sorted CD5+ B-1 cells from the peritoneal cavity lacked CD5 expression when cultured for 3 days in the presence but not absence of LPS, a stimuli that is known to induce IgM production by body cavity B-1 cells (Su et al., 1991) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the FACS data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: CD5 surface expression was unaffected during the first 2 cell divisions following LPS stimulation.
source: CD5 surface expression was unaffected during the first 2 cell divisions following stimulation, but was then quickly lost during the next 1–2 divisions (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the FACS data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: CD5 surface expression was quickly lost during the 3rd-4th cell divisions following LPS stimulation.
source: CD5 surface expression was unaffected during the first 2 cell divisions following stimulation, but was then quickly lost during the next 1–2 divisions (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the FACS data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Both surface-expressed CD5 and cd5 mRNA were decreased among B-1 cells after 3 days of LPS stimulation.
source: Both, surface-expressed CD5 and cd5 mRNA, as assessed by qRT-PCR, were decreased among B-1 cells after 3 days of LPS stimulation (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This is supported by the flow cytometry and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: Surface CD5 levels were decreased by 1.5 days of LPS culture.
source: Surface CD5 levels were decreased by 1.5 days of culture, while cd5 mRNA was not reduced until 2 days after culture onset (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: cd5 mRNA was not reduced until 2 days after LPS culture onset.
source: Surface CD5 levels were decreased by 1.5 days of culture, while cd5 mRNA was not reduced until 2 days after culture onset (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: LPS-stimulated B-1 cells began secreting IgM before CD5 levels were reduced.
source: The stimulated cells began secreting IgM before CD5 levels were reduced, but the increase in IgM secretion was more pronounced after 2 days of stimulation compared to the earlier time points (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by the ELISA data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The increase in IgM secretion was more pronounced after 2 days of LPS stimulation compared to earlier time points.
source: The stimulated cells began secreting IgM before CD5 levels were reduced, but the increase in IgM secretion was more pronounced after 2 days of stimulation compared to the earlier time points (Figure 2E).

claim: CD5- MedLN B-1 cells showed increased proliferation compared to their counterparts in body cavities after influenza infection.
